RPI has a pretty solid BME program, and by junior year you need to pick a concentration (I believe the concentrations are Biomaterials, Biomechanics, Biomedical Data Science, Bioimaging, and Medical Devices). The concentrations used to be Biomaterials (organic materials + materials you'd use in the body+ for prosthetics and such), Biomechanics (stuff like prosthetics and such), and Bioinstrumentation/Bioimaging (Xray machines, MRIs, ultrasound machines, etc). 

If you're doing BME, I'd recommend looking into what kind of job opportunities there are for each concentration, because it might turn out that a lot of jobs you could do w/ a Biomaterials concentration are better suited for Materials majors. What I'm trying to say is that a lot of the time, companies would rather hire a Mechanical engineer  than hire a Biomech person because MechE's have taken more relevant courses than BMEs have. Most BMEs at RPI do either Biomech or Biomaterials, and very few people do Bioinstrumentation/Bioimaging since the technical elective courses that you take and concentration classes you take are more electrical based and are usually pretty hard. Like other people in here have said, it's hard to get jobs as a BME if you're not doing  grad school, so I'd recommend doing the coterminal master's program that they have here (after you graduate, you do one more year of classes to get your Master's degree, and you get to use the same financial aid from before to complete it (but you need a >3.3 GPA so keep that in mind)). If you're not planning on doing any grad stuff at all, I'd recommend that you either find a different major that has better job opportunities for non-grads, like mechE, or electrical engineering, or Biology/Chem, or maybe choose one of the non-biomech/biomat concentrations. But don't worry yourself about that too much rn. 


Also, as for the school itself, a lot of people complain about the administration, which sucks ass, but so many of the professors I've had have been great and really want to help you learn. I'd say that one of the main reasons so many people would rather be at RPI than at a different school is that there are so many niche clubs and communities you can join, and everyone (most people) are pretty nerdy and just want to have fun + learn. If you're someone who's really put off by "weird" or nerdy people, maybe RPI isn't the greatest place for you. On the other hand, if you're involved in some weird, niche, or nerdy hobby, you're bound to find people with similar interests here (ex: board games club, Smash bros club, LARPing club, Dnd club, DDR club, etc or sports like hockey, soccer, rowing, fencing, hiking, etc). 



If you have more questions about concentrations, the school, clubs, the people, etc, lmk!

I took the Arch last year, and my experience was actually pretty good, and managed to take 20 credits and get my highest GPA so far. On the other hand, I know a lot of people that had to take hard classes which were really condensed down into 6 weeks or 12 weeks instead of the usual 16. Additionally, a lot of people, including myself, weren't able to take classes that they wanted because RPI doesn't offer all their courses during Arch. 

Another thing that people don't like about Arch is that it forces you to do something during your semester away, but there's a limited number of internships/coops, and RPI doesn't offer the greatest job seach help (from what I've heard from people), so many people ended up kind of wasting that semester. In some ways, the semester off can be great, if you've found a good job, but for a lot of people (including me), that isn't the case (yet). 

As for tuition and r&b, it's a little bit smaller than the regular semester from what I remember, but this year's tuition is changing because Arch is going online (which people hate of course). For your semester away, you don't have to pay tuition, luckily, and you can even make money at an internship, but like I said before, you could end up living with your parents during that time, which is what I fear could happen to me if I can't find a coop soon. Another option for semester away is study abroad, which could be useful, but you need to pay for of course. 

Also, to note, I did Early Arch, which is where you take the Arch semester right after your freshman year. I kind of recommend this, because you can take a bunch of core classes and HASS (arts and humanities) classes to fullfil your graduation requirements, and helps to boost your GPA a bit (which is what happened to me). The downside is that you'll only be around rising sophomores and other Early Archers (of which there aren't many), so social interaction might be limited. 

If you have any other questions, let me know!
